text: And if what you can't let in is kindness, when someone cares about you and it just bounces off, there's [Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy](https://www.apa.org/pubs/videos/4310759). The AEDP therapist stays with you through whatever comes up. When some of their kindness does get in, they ask what that's like and where you feel it in your body.
reader: an adult working through the guide who can feel their body by now but slips away from feelings in therapy sessions, deciding whether to look for one of these therapists, which one, and how to vet one

checked.point: ISTDP points out avoidance as it happens and turns the patient back toward the feeling; anxiety about the feeling drives the avoidance; the therapist watches it in tense muscles, sighing and foggy thinking; most patients have low anxiety tolerance and get a graded, slower format
checked.still_needed: yes: they picture a session and know they won't be pushed past what they can take

checked.point: APT treats fear of one's own feelings like a phobia, with gradual exposure to the feeling
checked.still_needed: yes: they recognize their case and know the pace is set by what they can bear

checked.point: AEDP undoes aloneness, helps the patient take in the therapist's care, asks about taking it in, and tracks the feeling in the body
checked.found: APA, Fosha (https://www.apa.org/pubs/videos/4310759); AEDP Institute, "enhancing receptive capacity" and "processing relational affects" (https://aedpinstitute.org/?p=552), "focusing on the physical experience of emotion" (https://aedpinstitute.org/?p=254), the patient's capacity "to take in the therapist's presence, support and care" (https://aedpinstitute.org/journal/making-good-use-of-suffering-intra-relational-work-with-pathogenic-affects/)
checked.still_needed: yes: they picture what the therapy does with care that bounces off

placement: fourth: the third therapy, by its case

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
